source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: multiple choice calibration
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice when the options are shown in a lettered format. Calibration improves with model size and from zero-shot to few-shot.
numbers: Tasks: BIG-Bench, MMLU and others; models up to 52B.
limits: Replacing an option with 'none of the above' cut accuracy and calibration significantly.
agent_relevance: Format matters. Ask for confidence over a visible list of options, not in free text.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) P(True) self-evaluation
finding: Models can judge whether their own samples are true or false, but this is harder because models find their own samples plausible. Few-shot self-evaluation is calibrated; zero-shot is not. Larger k mostly helps calibration, not AUROC.
numbers: Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, HumanEval, arithmetic, function synthesis. Showing many T=1 samples with the one to grade improved results.
limits: Similar in spirit to self-consistency. Calibration can be fixed by examples; discrimination cannot.
agent_relevance: Do not trust zero-shot self-grading (matches G2 and G4). Self-grade only with shown samples.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) RLHF miscalibration and temperature
finding: RLHF policies look miscalibrated on MMLU, MMLU true/false and TruthfulQA, but a simple temperature adjustment makes them fairly well calibrated.
numbers: 52B, 5-shot; curves shown at T=1 and T=2.5.
limits: This is token probability, not verbal confidence. Later work (Leng 2025) finds RLHF inflates verbalized confidence.
agent_relevance: If we log confidence, fit a recalibration map on our own data rather than trust raw numbers.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) P(IK) trained self-knowledge
finding: Models trained to predict P(IK), the chance they know the answer, do well in distribution and partly generalise, but are poorly calibrated on new tasks. P(IK) rose with relevant source material and with hints on GSM8k.
numbers: Ground truth P(IK) is the fraction of unit-temperature samples that are correct; 52B model.
limits: Ranking transfers better than calibration.
agent_relevance: Recalibrate per task family; do not carry one confidence map across domains.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 was finetuned to state its confidence in words or numbers and was moderately calibrated, also under distribution shift. This was the first demonstration of verbalized probability.
numbers: CalibratedMath: 21 arithmetic tasks; trained on Add-subtract, tested on Multiply-divide and Multi-answer; GPT-3 175B. Score is MSE of the stated probability.
limits: Meaningless label names worked slightly better than words like 'low'. Needed finetuning in 2022.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only scaffold cannot rely on this. Use sampling-based checks instead.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Verbalized probability vs logit baselines
finding: Verbalized probability beat the zero-shot answer logit and a finetuned indirect logit on MSE under shift. The authors give evidence it uses pre-trained latent representations of epistemic uncertainty, not just copied logits.
numbers: A constant baseline (using training-set accuracy) is included; on the Multiply-divide set, where accuracy shifted little, it was competitive.
limits: A constant baseline is strong when accuracy does not shift, so gains must be judged against it.
agent_relevance: Always test our confidence guardrail against a constant-rate baseline.

source: Xiong et al. (2024, ICLR) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? vanilla verbalized confidence
finding: Vanilla verbalized confidence is highly overconfident and poor at ranking right from wrong. GPT-4 average AUROC was 62.7 across 8 datasets, near the 50 chance level.
numbers: Models: GPT-3, Vicuna, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA 2; 8 datasets (GSM8K, SVAMP, Date, Count, Strategy, Sport, Law, Ethics). Average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
limits: Confidence values cluster at the high end, in 80 to 100 percent.
agent_relevance: Do not act on a bare verbalized confidence in our agent.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Prompt strategies lower ECE but not failure prediction
finding: Human-inspired prompts (CoT, multi-step, top-K) lower ECE but failure prediction stays close to random. The ECE drop came mainly from shrinking the gap between mean confidence and accuracy.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-4 with 93.6% accuracy got ECE 0.064 by assigning 100% confidence to every sample.
limits: Metric trap: a constant high answer scores well on ECE when accuracy is high.
agent_relevance: Judge our guardrail on AUROC or Brier, not ECE alone.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Sampling consistency vs verbalized confidence
finding: Agreement among sampled answers predicts failure far better than verbalized confidence. On GSM8K AUROC rose from 54.8% to 92.7% with 5 samples and consistency aggregation.
numbers: Gains grow with number of samples M (1 to 13) then flatten; cost is linear in M. White-box methods were only modestly better (AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605).
limits: No method won everywhere. All struggled on tasks needing professional knowledge (law, ethics).
agent_relevance: Use agreement among attempts as the signal, but treat it as a hint (G4: samples are correlated).

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: verbal vs token probabilities
finding: For RLHF models, verbalized confidence is often better calibrated than token probabilities, often cutting ECE by a relative 50% or more.
numbers: ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 1 and 2, Llama-2-70B-chat; TriviaQA and SciQ with 1000 questions each, TruthfulQA with 817. gpt-3.5 on TriviaQA: label prob ECE 0.140, 'Is True' prob ECE 0.164, Verb. 1S top-1 ECE 0.068.
limits: Claude-1 verbalized worse than GPT models though its token probabilities were similar. This conflicts with Xiong on the size of overconfidence: easy trivia vs hard reasoning, different prompts and metrics.
agent_relevance: Task type decides whether verbal numbers are usable. Check on our own tasks.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Considering alternatives before stating confidence
finding: Asking for k guesses with a probability each, in one reply, improved calibration. Two-stage with CoT was worse than top-k. This echoes the human 'consider the opposite' debiasing result.
numbers: gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE: Verb. 1S top-1 0.068, top-2 0.050, top-4 0.054; Verb. 2S CoT 0.110, 2S top-2 0.047.
limits: Gain levels off after about two guesses. CoT alone did not help here.
agent_relevance: Ask for two ranked alternatives with probabilities before committing a confidence.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Linguistic expressions of confidence
finding: Words like 'highly likely', mapped to numbers by a human survey table or by a held-out optimum, gave calibration similar to stated numbers.
numbers: gpt-3.5 TriviaQA: Ling. 1S-human ECE 0.062, Ling. 1S-opt ECE 0.058; AUC about 0.88.
limits: Mapping was fixed from human values; the models use few distinct phrases.
agent_relevance: Prefer a small fixed ladder of words, with the mapping checked on our own data.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky, Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the Grey Area
finding: Epistemic markers inserted in the prompt change accuracy strongly: up to 80% change on the same questions. Certainty markers lowered accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3 davinci, 50 markers, 4 datasets. Weakeners averaged 47% accuracy vs 40% for strengtheners. Prefix 'I think it's' gave 63% vs 80% as a suffix. 21 of 28 templates with 100% scored lower; accuracy peaked at 70 to 90%.
limits: Corpus study: certainty words appear mostly in questions, uncertainty words in answers. Models may copy usage patterns, a rival to the claim that they track knowledge. Only GPT-3 era models.
agent_relevance: Avoid certainty words in instructions to the model; 'be sure' may lower accuracy.

source: Mielke et al. (2022) Reducing conversational agents' overconfidence through linguistic calibration
finding: A chit-chat bot (BlenderBot) sounded confident but was mostly wrong: it answered 29.45% of questions confidently, and only 14% of its confident answers were correct.
numbers: TriviaQA, human-annotated correctness and linguistic confidence. Vanilla accuracy was about 5.0% on the valid set.
limits: A separate calibrator that predicts correctness, plus controllable generation, improved linguistic calibration. Old small model.
agent_relevance: Decouple the confidence estimate from the text style: a separate predictor sets the words.

source: Yona, Aharoni, Geva (2024) Can LLMs Faithfully Express Their Intrinsic Uncertainty in Words?
finding: LLMs hedge when confident and answer decisively when unsure. Faithfulness (match of hedge to consistency-based confidence) stays low even after prompting.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini Nano/Pro/Ultra; PopQA and Natural Questions. Prompting raised the score to at most 0.63 (GPT-4) and 0.7 (Gemini Ultra) from a 0.5 baseline. Decisiveness vs confidence correlation was weak.
limits: Confidence is measured from answer consistency across samples; decisiveness is scored by an LLM prompt that agreed with human survey data.
agent_relevance: Do not read the hedging words in the model's prose as a signal.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs Know and What People Think They Know: gaps
finding: People overrate LLM answers given default explanations (calibration gap) and cannot tell right from wrong (discrimination gap). Model confidence discriminated at AUC 0.75 to 0.78; humans got 0.59 to 0.60.
numbers: 301 Prolific participants; MMLU multiple choice with GPT-3.5 and PaLM2, short-answer TriviaQA with GPT-4o. Model AUC: 0.751, 0.746, 0.781. Human AUC: 0.589, 0.602, 0.592.
limits: Human error was mainly overconfidence on multiple choice. Participants lacked domain knowledge: when they changed the answer it was 33% right vs 39% for the LLM.
agent_relevance: If a human reads our output, wording drives trust more than content does.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) Explanation length and aligned uncertainty language
finding: Longer explanations raised human confidence without better discrimination. Matching low, medium or high uncertainty language to the model's own confidence narrowed both gaps, but human decision accuracy did not improve.
numbers: Experiments 2a to 2c, n=60, 60, 59. Long vs short explanation BF=25; mean human AUC 0.54 (long) vs 0.57 (uncertainty only). Wording effect BF>100.
limits: Better confidence wording changed belief, not final accuracy, since people had little independent knowledge.
agent_relevance: Verbal confidence helps routing and abstaining, not making answers more correct. Keep answers short.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) LLMs Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know: fine-tuned graders
finding: Prompting alone gives poor uncertainty. Fine-tuning a correctness classifier (LoRA plus prompt) on about 1000 graded examples beat black-box baselines on ECE and AUROC.
numbers: LLaMA-2 7B/13B and Mistral 7B, MMLU multiple choice and open-ended. Frozen-feature probes were worse than LoRA. Perplexity did not predict correctness in open-ended generation.
limits: Open-source 7B-13B models only; MMLU only.
agent_relevance: A separate grader can supply confidence. We need not trust the generator's own words.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Transfer across topics, formats and models
finding: Learned uncertainty estimates transferred across subject areas, formats and even other models. Mistral 7B had higher AUROC on LLaMA-2 7B outputs than LLaMA-2 7B had on itself.
numbers: Training set had near zero social science examples yet performance was similar across categories.
limits: Argues against special self-knowledge; the signal appears to be general question-answer fit.
agent_relevance: A different model as grader may be as good or better than self-report (links to G4: use different models if possible).

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) User study of confidence use
finding: In a human-AI exam, users followed informative confidence scores; with zero-shot confidence the scores gave little signal.
numbers: N=181 Prolific participants, 20 per variant, 60 MMLU questions per batch, Mistral 7B Instruct.
limits: Preliminary; small cells; MMLU only.
agent_relevance: Confidence is only worth showing once it is calibrated.

source: Leng et al. (2025, ICLR) Taming Overconfidence in LLMs: Reward Calibration in RLHF
finding: RLHF raises verbalized overconfidence because reward models prefer high-confidence answers regardless of quality. Vanilla PPO worsened calibration while raising accuracy relative to SFT.
numbers: Llama3-8B and Mistral-7B, six datasets. PPO-M and PPO-C lowered ECE and raised AUC; calibrated DPO cut ECE by over 50%.
limits: Only two 7-8B models; the fix needs training.
agent_relevance: Assume chat models inflate stated confidence. Our scaffold must discount it.

source: Yoon et al. (2025, NeurIPS) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Reasoning models were better calibrated than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings. The gain comes from slow thinking: trying alternatives and backtracking.
numbers: 6 reasoning models, 6 datasets. GLM-Z1 had 0.07 lower accuracy than GLM-4 on NonambigQA but 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC. Qwen3 shows the gap between thinking and non-thinking mode in one checkpoint.
limits: A few cases where the non-reasoning model had better AUROC (for example GLM-4 on both Math subsets). Calibration got better as the CoT unfolded; removing slow-thinking behaviour hurt; in-context slow thinking helped non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Report confidence at the end of an alternatives-and-verify pass, not before it (fits G1).

source: Damani et al. (2026, ICLR) Beyond Binary Rewards: RLCR
finding: Training on a correctness reward alone worsens calibration. Adding a Brier-score term keeps accuracy and sharply cuts ECE.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B with GRPO. In-domain ECE on HotpotQA 0.37 to 0.03; on math datasets 0.26 to 0.10. Binary RL made out-of-domain calibration worse; RLCR improved it.
limits: One 7B base model; requires training.
agent_relevance: Binary rewards teach guessing. Any selection step we run should reward abstention or low confidence when wrong.

source: Belem et al. (2024) Perceptions of Linguistic Uncertainty by Language Models and Humans
finding: 7 of 10 LLMs map words like 'probably' to numbers like humans do, but their numbers shift with whether the statement is true or false.
numbers: 10 models. For the 6 best, mean response was 7.0 points lower for false statements; for 'possible' the gap was 49.5 points. GPT-4, Llama3 70B and Gemini matched the human modal response at 85% or more.
limits: Prior-knowledge bias exceeds that of humans. Replicated with 400 extra statements (all but Gemma 2B).
agent_relevance: LLMs mix the speaker's confidence with their own belief. Translate hedges to numbers in code before the model reads them.

source: Lichtenstein, Fischhoff, Phillips (1982) Calibration of probabilities: the state of the art to 1980
finding: Classic review: people are overconfident on hard general-knowledge questions, and the effect shrinks or reverses on easy ones (hard-easy effect). Background from memory; not opened.
numbers: Not checked this session.
limits: Not opened. Later work reads the hard-easy effect partly as regression and noise.
agent_relevance: Report calibration split by difficulty.

source: Moore & Healy (2008) The trouble with overconfidence
finding: Separates overestimation, overplacement and overprecision; hard tasks give overestimation but underplacement. Background from memory; not opened.
numbers: Not checked this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Separate the confidence-vs-accuracy gap from comparing against others.

source: Wallsten, Budescu and colleagues (1986 onward) verbal probability phrases
finding: Verbal probability phrases vary in numeric meaning between people and with context, but are more stable within a person. Background from memory; cited in Belem 2024; not opened.
numbers: Not checked this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Use a fixed word ladder, not free hedges.
